'''Nen''' (Nen Zi, Nenium, Wekamara) is a [[Yam languages|Yam]] language spoken in the Bimadbn village in the [[Western Province (Papua New Guinea)|Western Province]] of [[Papua New Guinea]], with 250 speakers as of a 2002 [[SIL International|SIL]] survey. It is situated between the speech communities of [[Nambu language|Nambu]] and [[Idi language|Idi]].

Nen has unusual lexicalization patterns in its verbs. It has very few intransitive verbs, and where some verbs would be intransitive in most other languages, Nen has a class of morphologically "middle" verbs in their place. Many of the few intransitive verbs that Nen does have are positional verbs, which refer to spatial positions and postures.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Evans |first=Nicholas |date=2014 |title=Positional Verbs in Nen |journal=Oceanic Linguistics |language=en |volume=53 |issue=2 |pages=225–255 |doi=10.1353/ol.2014.0019|hdl=1885/14019 |hdl-access=free }}</ref>

== Morphology ==

=== Number ===
The realization of different grammatical meanings of Number in the noun depends on the syntactic function and case marking. The noun in the dative overtly differentiates 4 grammatical meaning of number: singular, dual, paucal and plural; the noun in the oblique shows singular ~ dual ~ paucal/plural opposition, while the [[Ergative case|ergative]] '''−''' [[Grammatical number|singular]] ~ [[dual (grammatical number)|dual]]/[[paucal]] ~ [[plural]], and the noun in [[Absolutive case|absolutive]] cannot be distinguished according to number.<ref name="valency">{{harvp|Evans|2015}}</ref>

=== Direction ===
The verb expresses three grammatical meaning of motion: neutral − /Ø-/, towards speaker /n-/, and away from speaker /ng-/: ''n-'''Ø'''-armbte'' '(s)he is ascending' ~ ''n-'''n'''-armbte'' '(s)he is coming up (towards speaker) ~ ''n-'''ng'''-armbte'' '(s)he is going up (away from speaker).<ref name="valency" />{{rp|1056}}

== Syntax ==
The constituent order in clause is [[Subject–object–verb|SOV]]. Case marking shows ergative/absolutive alignment.<ref name="valency" />

=== Argument structure and valency ===
According to indexing, the verbs can be either prefixing (an undergoer argument is cross-referenced by a prefix) or ambifixing (arguments are cross-referenced by both prefix and suffix in the verb). In the transitive predicate, a verbal prefix expresses patient and a verbal suffix '''−''' actor. There are several types of valency pattern in Nen:<ref name="valency" />{{rp|1058–68}}

'''1.''' Basically monovalent pattern
* Basic intransitive − NP<sub>abs</sub> U-V
* Intrinsic middle − NP<sub>abs</sub> M-V-A
* Middle with cognate object − NP<sub>abs</sub> + NP<sub>abs</sub> M-V-A
'''2.''' Basically divalent pattern
* Basic transitive − NP<sub>erg</sub> + NP<sub>abs</sub> U-V-A
* Experiencer object construction − NP<sub>abs</sub> > NP<sub>erg</sub> U-V-A<sub>3sg</sub>
* Transitive verbs with deponent middle verbal morphology − N<sub>perg</sub> + NP<sub>abs</sub> M-V-A
* Semi-transitive verb registering oblique on undergoer slot − NP<sub>erg</sub> + NP<sub>obl</sub> U-V-A
'''3.''' Trivalent pattern

The arguments get the following case marking: the subject − ergative, the direct object − absolutive, and the indirect object − dative. In a trivalent predicate, the indirect object argument (semantically, recipient) is cross-referenced in the verb by the undergoer prefix.<ref name="valency" />{{rp|1067–68}}

=== Causative ===
Middle verbs form their [[causative]] using a prefix {{IPA|/wa-/}}, which may be glossed 'to cause (motion/trajectory) through sustained contact (carrying, leading etc.)'. The resulting form follows [[Ergativity|ergative syntax]].<ref name="valency" />

=== Benefactive ===
Beneficiary is expressed by the undergoer prefix.<ref name="valency" />{{rp|1058–68}}
